A laser technician is reducing the diagonals of a square aperture at a rate of $2.4\text{ mm}\text{/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the aperture decreasing when the diagonals are $12.5\,\text{mm}$ long each?

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The area is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$
question.worked_solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $h$ decreases at a rate of $2.4\,\text{mm/s},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-2.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the area when the diagonal has length $h=12.5.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-2.4\cdot 12.5=-30{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area of the square aperture is decreasing at a rate of $30{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$
